Need to search first.I've written verse-by-verse notes for Acts 5:1–21, but the research tool hit its usage limit partway through, so some parts are missing. I fully read three sources: Enduring Word, Ellicott (whose page stops around v. 17) and Wesley's Notes. The rest comes from the short excerpts that search results show, which I've marked as "(excerpt)". I didn't get to the Catholic and Orthodox pages, the modern-scholarship sites, or prosperity and word-of-faith teaching, so those are missing or very thin, as your brief asked.

**Sources** (short names used in the notes)
- EW = https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-5/ (David Guzik, who quotes Bruce, Boice, Morgan, Stott and others)
- ELL = https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/acts/5.htm (Ellicott, Anglican)
- WES = https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/acts/5.htm and https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/acts-5.html (Wesley, Methodist)
- GILL = https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/acts-5.html (Gill, Baptist; excerpt)
- PA = https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-5-commentary (excerpt)
- SL3 = https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/5-3.html (several commentators; excerpt)
- BH1 = https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/5-1.htm (several commentators; excerpt)

---

## 1. The traditional reading, verse by verse

**v. 1**
- This follows straight on from Barnabas's gift in 4:36–37. The couple wanted the same respect he got. (EW)
- The chapter break is badly placed, since the verse begins with "But." When pressure from outside failed, Satan switched to corrupting the church from inside. The names are ironic: Ananias means "Jehovah is gracious," and he didn't live up to it. (PA)
- Ananias wanted Barnabas's praise "more cheaply." It was an attempt to serve God and money at once, and to have a saint's reputation without real holiness. Ellicott compares it to Gehazi's sin, but says it was against greater light. (ELL)

**v. 2**
- The Greek verb for "kept back" means to misappropriate. The Greek Old Testament uses it for Achan's theft (Joshua 7). Bruce: Ananias is to Acts what Achan is to Joshua. Bruce also suggests they may have vowed the whole amount. (EW)
- Keeping money back was not wrong in itself. The problem was offering part as if it were the whole, which Ellicott calls "an acted lie." (ELL)
- Ananias had announced that he sold the land for the church's use, then kept part back. (GILL)
- One commentary on BH1 sees a double fraud: passing off part as the whole, and implying they had the same claim on the shared fund as people who had nothing. (BH1)

**v. 3**
- Peter knew what had happened by supernatural insight, which Guzik identifies with the "word of knowledge" of 1 Cor 12:8. Quoting Stott, he says a public sin was dealt with publicly. (EW)
- Like Judas, the evil came from Satan. Peter's question "why" implies Ananias could have resisted. Ellicott weighs two meanings of "lie to the Holy Spirit" and notes a change in the Greek wording between vv. 3 and 4. (ELL)
- Clarke: the Greek word was used for embezzling public money. Barnes: he was "tempting" God, as if God couldn't detect the fraud. Constable: greed lies behind many of the failures in Acts. (SL3)
- Chrysostom calls Peter's knowledge a miracle even greater than the earlier ones. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/210112.htm (excerpt)

**v. 4**
- The money was entirely theirs. The sin was the deception, not keeping money back. Satan can influence even a Spirit-filled believer, but he "can't do your sinning for you." (EW)
- No church rule required the gift. He would have been blameless giving part as part, or nothing at all. Setting "lied to the Holy Spirit" (v. 3) beside "lied to God" (v. 4) is a fair proof that the Spirit is God. (ELL)
- Same point on the Spirit's deity; Steven Cole adds that giving nothing would not have been a sin. (PA)
- He might have kept it all, or given whatever share he pleased. (GILL)

**v. 5**
- Peter pronounced no sentence; the death was God's act (Morgan). Guzik suggests shock as the physical cause, and says the wonder is that God usually delays judgment. Orr: revival is "like Judgment Day." (EW)
- Ellicott sees natural causes and God's purpose working together: shame at being found out was enough to kill him. He adds a caution: there is a "silence" about anything beyond the visible judgment. (ELL)
- The severity was just, and also wise and kind, because it would deter others and confirm the apostles' honesty. (WES)

**v. 6**
- "Young men" means the younger men, as a group distinct from the elders. Ellicott sees here the beginnings of the later office of deacon. Quick burial was the custom, and treating the body with respect showed reverence for it. (ELL)

**v. 7**
- She knew about the fraud but not that it had been found out. Gill finds it striking that she hadn't heard the news within three hours. (GILL)

**v. 8**
- Peter's question gave her a chance to repent. She had already failed to stop her husband, and now she missed this chance too. (ELL)
- Constable: Peter didn't mention her husband's death because he wanted the truth from her. (PA)

**v. 9**
- "Test the Spirit" means testing whether the Spirit in the apostles really could see into hearts. "Spirit of the Lord" carries its Old Testament sense. (ELL)
- Submission within marriage never extends to joining in sin. (EW)

**v. 10**
- Same sin, same judgment. (EW)
- Peter's question was a final chance to tell the truth. (PA)

**v. 11**
- This is the first time Acts uses the word "church" (*ekklesia*). The fear made some draw near with reverence and others hold back in awe. (ELL)
- Wesley describes a New Testament church as people called by the gospel, joined to Christ by baptism, united in love, and disciplined by this event. (WES)
- Hackett: the event is a lasting warning in every age. (PA)
- In Joshua the people carried out the judgment; here God did it himself. So the church should not punish people this way. (EW)

**v. 12**
- This answers the prayer for signs and wonders in 4:30. Being "of one accord" is itself a sign of the Spirit's power. (EW)
- Solomon's Porch was a favourite place for teachers. (ELL)
- Vance Havner: miracles are not the foundation of Christian life; the resurrection is. (PA)

**v. 13**
- The church's seriousness cut down casual commitment. (EW)
- Ellicott thinks "the rest" probably means Pharisees and other teachers who sympathised but lacked courage. (ELL)
- Wesley: it means formalists and hypocrites. (WES)
- Gill: it means church members, even ministers, who kept a respectful distance from the apostles. (GILL)
- Havner: when the church takes a stand, it repels careless "joiners." (PA)

**v. 14**
- New believers were added "to the Lord," meaning to God himself, not to a movement. The growth shows the purging did no lasting harm. (EW)
- "Lord" means the Lord Jesus. Mentioning women is typical of Luke. (ELL)
- True believers increased because unbelievers stayed away. (WES)
- "Added to the Lord" means added to the church, of which Christ is head. (GILL)

**v. 15**
- The text doesn't actually say the shadow healed anyone, only that people believed it would. If it did, the shadow was a "point of contact" for faith, like the hem of Jesus' garment. Stott notes that Luke's verb "overshadow" is used of God's presence. Marshall notes that people in the ancient world thought shadows had magical power. (EW)
- Ellicott disagrees: v. 16 implies their hope was not disappointed. He compares Paul's handkerchiefs (19:12) and says any medium can help faith. (ELL)

**v. 16**
- This is the first sign of the work spreading beyond Jerusalem. But people came to the apostles rather than the apostles going out, as Acts 1:8 commanded. (EW)
- The verb tense shows it went on day after day, probably for months. (ELL)

**v. 17**
- The high priest was probably Annas or Caiaphas. Ellicott says the note that they were Sadducees is very important: they denied the resurrection the apostles preached. (ELL)
- Wesley calls their zeal "angry, bitter, persecuting zeal." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/5-17.html
- The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary says the word means "hot, angry zeal," not envy. (same page)

**v. 18**
- This time all the apostles were arrested, and it wasn't the first arrest (see 4:3). (EW)

**v. 19**
- Angels serve God's people (Hebrews 1:14). Hughes points out the "divine humor": the Sadducees didn't believe in angels. (EW)

**v. 20**
- They were freed to keep working, not for their own comfort. Later, most apostles were not rescued and died as martyrs. (EW)
- The angel's message was "Explain," not "Escape." (PA)

**v. 21**
- Toussaint lists the ironies: guards protecting empty cells, and the court gathering to judge prisoners it didn't have. (PA)

## 2. Where Protestant traditions differ

**Were Ananias and Sapphira believers? (vv. 1, 5, 10)**
- **Methodist:** Wesley says Ananias was "certainly" not a believer, because all believers were of one heart. He was probably not baptized yet. (WES)
- **Nonconformist (Matthew Henry):** they wanted to seem leading disciples when they weren't true disciples. (BH1)
- **Reformed (Boice, quoted by Guzik):** "true Christians do not lose their salvation"; the punishment was for this life only. (EW)
- **Guzik:** only God knows. He points to the "sin unto death" in 1 John 5 and 1 Cor 11. (EW)
- **Anglican (Ellicott):** we must keep silent beyond the visible judgment. He compares 1 Cor 5:5, where the flesh is destroyed so the spirit may be saved. (ELL)

**Was the sharing of goods expected? (vv. 3–4)**
- **Wesley:** every Christian with land sold it. Ananias's act was "the first attempt to bring" private ownership into the church. (WES)
- **Others:** the sharing was voluntary. Meyer (on BH1) calls it "simply permissive"; see also ELL and GotQuestions (https://www.gotquestions.org/Ananias-and-Sapphira.html).

**Peter's shadow (v. 15)**
- **Guzik:** the text doesn't say it healed; at most it was a point of contact for faith. (EW)
- **Ellicott:** healing did follow. (ELL)
- I didn't get to read the Pentecostal sites (ag.org, pneumareview.com).

## 3. Other views (very limited)
- **Chrysostom (Church Father):** the aggravating factor was that the sin was planned together in secret. He also says Ananias was blinded by greed. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/210112.htm (excerpt)
- **Ancient background:** the only scholarly note I have is Marshall, quoted by Guzik, on ancient beliefs about shadows (see v. 15). (EW)
- **Not found:** anything on catholic.com, oca.org, netbible.org or bibleodyssey.org, and nothing on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace readings.

MacArthur's sermon at https://www.gty.org/library/sermons-library/44-20/when-sin-entered-the-church-part-2 only came through as an outline (sinful pretense, spiritual perception), so I left it out of the notes.
